# Answer key - Chapter 04: Networking and firewall controls {.unnumbered}

**Q1** *(tests @sec-04-addresses-ports-attack-surface · basic)* - **Correct: b.**
The chapter states that the pair *(address, port)* "names one service on one
machine"; an IP address alone identifies only the machine (a), and virtual
networks (c) and rules (d) are different concepts from the same chapter.

**Q2** *(tests @sec-04-cloud-networks-software · basic)* - **Correct: a.**
The chapter says security groups are stateful and attach to resources,
whereas NACLs work lower in the stack, are typically stateless and apply to
subnets (CSA, 2024, p. 156); the other options invert or merge the two.

**Q3** *(tests @sec-04-cloud-networks-software · basic)* - **Accepted answers:**
"AWS starts from deny-all, so even resources in the same security group
cannot talk until a rule permits it; Azure's NSG default rules allow traffic
freely within the virtual network while denying inbound from the Internet",
"Azure is open east–west inside the VNet by default, AWS denies everything
by default" (any phrasing capturing both defaults plus the point that
assuming the wrong default leaves a service reachable from an unintended
place).

**Q4** *(tests @sec-04-the-firewall · basic)* - **Correct: c.**
Default-deny means the final catch-all rule blocks everything not explicitly
permitted (@def-firewall); (a) is default-allow, (b) is no policy at all,
and (d) is wrong because the laboratory firewalls are stateful, so replies
return without a separate rule.

**Q5** *(tests @sec-04-firewall-types-ngfw-waf · basic)* - **Accepted answers:**
any two of: "deep packet inspection / looking inside the payload",
"identifying the application in a flow", "rules by user identity rather
than only by address", "integrated intrusion prevention (IPS)",
"consulting threat-intelligence feeds of known-bad addresses and domains".

**Q6** *(tests @sec-04-defence-in-depth-zero-trust · basic)* - **Correct: b.**
This is @def-zerotrust almost verbatim; (a) is the traditional
castle-and-moat perimeter the Guidance rejects, (c) is not a described
strategy, and (d) contradicts "nobody is trusted for having logged in once".

**Q7 - applied scenario** *(tests @sec-04-the-firewall · applied)* -
**Model answer:** the answer must identify (i) the forgotten database
port 5432 - the chapter's second common mistake ("opening a database port
for testing and forgetting it"); (ii) SSH open to the whole Internet instead
of only the administrator's address - the first mistake and the risk of
@exm-ssh-trc; and (iii) the Azure default - the third mistake ("assuming
closed when the default is open"): the NSG's built-in rules allow east–west
traffic within the virtual network, so other VNet resources may reach the VM
even without added allow rules. The command sequence:
`sudo ufw default deny incoming`, `sudo ufw default allow outgoing`,
`sudo ufw allow from YOUR_IP to any port 22 proto tcp`,
`sudo ufw allow 80/tcp`, `sudo ufw enable`, then `sudo ufw status` to read
the loaded policy back. Grading notes: full credit needs all three
exposures, the restricted SSH rule (not the blanket `allow 22/tcp`), no
rule for 5432, and ideally the read-back with `ufw status`; partial credit
for two exposures or a sequence missing the defaults/read-back.

## Sketch answers to the chapter exercises

**(1)** *(→ @exr-04-attack-surface, "Attack surface")*
The attack surface is every point an attacker can interact with: open
ports, reachable services, exposed endpoints; `ss -tulpn` enumerates the
listening ports, so it measures that surface and allows each door to be
justified.

**(2)** *(→ @exr-04-default-deny-reasoning, "Default-deny reasoning")*
Default-deny blocks everything except explicitly permitted
traffic; like the MVN, it works by listing the few legitimate flows and
forbidding the rest, which needs no knowledge of the attacker.

**(3)** *(→ @exr-04-cloud-firewall-default, "A cloud firewall default")*
Azure's network security groups allow east–west traffic within the virtual
network by default (while denying inbound from the Internet), so intra-VNet
paths may be open even when no rule was added; on AWS a security group
denies all inbound traffic, including between resources in the same group,
until it is allowed. The mental model is the same, namely know the default
before trusting it, and assuming the wrong one can leave a resource
reachable from an unintended location.

**(4)** *(→ @exr-04-ngfw-vs-waf, "NGFW vs WAF")*
An NGFW secures the network broadly with application awareness
and deep packet inspection; a WAF secures one web application by inspecting
HTTP requests, so against an application-layer flood on the login page the
WAF applies (Session 8).

**(5)** *(→ @exr-04-ssh-brute-force-trc, "SSH brute force as threat–risk–control")*
Threat: automated brute-forcing of the SSH login.
Risk: high likelihood (constant scanning), high impact (full control on
success). Control: restrict SSH to the administrative address with
`sudo ufw allow from YOUR_IP to any port 22 proto tcp`.
